notes.meaning: The writer identifies himself simply as the elder, a title suited to the Apostle John because of his advanced age and his pastoral care. He writes to Gaius, a dear Christian friend whom he loves in the shared bond of the gospel truth. Gaius was a very common Roman name, though he was known for his genuine faith and generous spirit.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that the letter was not written by the Apostle John, but by a distinct church leader known as John the Presbyter or John the Elder.

notes.meaning: The apostle expresses an affectionate prayer that Gaius may enjoy good bodily health and succeed in his daily life, just as his spiritual life is already flourishing. John already knew that Gaius was strong in faith, which made his healthy soul the standard for this friendly greeting.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern prosperity teachers take this verse as a divine promise that God guarantees physical health and financial wealth to every faithful believer, though other commentators view it merely as a customary, polite letter greeting.

notes.meaning: Visiting believers brought reports back to John about Gaius's steady faith and consistent life. John felt deep joy upon hearing that Gaius was continually putting the truth into practice in daily action.

Nothing brings greater happiness to a devoted pastor or spiritual father than knowing his spiritual children are living out God's truth. True faith is more than correct belief; it is shown by how one lives each day.

John commends Gaius for his faithful service in showing hospitality to travelling Christians. This kindness was especially admirable because these travelling workers were complete strangers to him personally.

These travelling workers spoke openly to John's home church about the warm love Gaius showed them. John encourages him to keep helping them on their travels with supplies in a manner that truly honours God.
These missionaries went out into the world purely to spread the name and work of Jesus Christ. They chose not to ask for or accept any financial support from the unbelievers to whom they preached.

Because these missionaries took no money from outsiders, other Christians have a duty to welcome and care for them. By providing food, shelter, and travel funds, believers become full partners in spreading the truth of the gospel.

John had sent a letter of recommendation to the local congregation, but a leader named Diotrephes refused to accept the apostle's guidance. Diotrephes was driven by selfish pride and craved the chief place of power over the church.

If John visits, he intends to confront Diotrephes publicly for spreading spiteful and empty slander against the apostles. Not stopped by mere bad talk, Diotrephes also refused to welcome travelling missionaries, stopped others from helping them, and expelled hospitable members from the church.

Gaius is urged not to follow the bad example of Diotrephes, but to copy what is good and loving. Those who practice goodness show that they belong to God, while those who persist in harmful and arrogant behavior show they do not really know Him.

In contrast to Diotrephes, Demetrius has earned an excellent reputation among all who know him. His upright life matches the standard of God's truth, and John adds his own reliable apostolic endorsement of Demetrius's character.

John has much more that needs to be addressed regarding these church matters, but he chooses not to write them down with pen and ink. Putting sensitive matters into writing might cause misunderstandings or fall into the wrong hands.

John plans to visit Gaius very soon so they can discuss everything directly in person. He ends with a traditional blessing of peace, passing along warm greetings from local Christian friends and asking Gaius to greet each faithful friend individually by name.
